Spoiler-free review.

[b]Technical[/b] 
Finally a console ported game worth buying on pc - in three playthroughs I've only run into two crashes and a couple of glitches here and there. The game's well polished and not the buggy mess, I've come to expect by now, when going for AAA games. I suppose it helps, that the game has been out on console for ages now and yes, also running top end hardware. Nevertheless I'm usually very sceptical when it comes to ported games. Hence: BRAVO.

[b]Story[/b] 
Complemented with the soundtrack and visuals, the story was absolutely breathtaking. Been a long time I invested emotionally into a game. Give them writers a raise :) Even on third playthrough I still had shivers running down my back on some scenes.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The (story) missions themselves are pretty linear, with some hidden side rooms, if you want to explore and get some background infos to the lore/history. The map is, after a first/short walled of segment, open. Side missions and objectives scattered all over the place. Its left up to the player, how he wants to deal with the world. You ain't forced into specific areas and not even forced to complete every side quest. Overall you can get around 80 hours of gameplay, if you want to collect all, listen to all datapoints and so on. If you just focus on the main-missions, I estimate it'll last 40+ hrs ez.

[b]Price[/b] 
Well worth the 60 bucks on pc.

[b]Addendum[/b] 
I don't expect Sony's gonna read this, but just in case: This game was one of my favorite games this year. I'd even hand over more of my hard earned $$$ for quality products like this. I will not buy a console however, just to get access to exclusive games - even if they all as good as this one (looking at you there "God of War" or "The Last of us"). So why don't you do us all, and frankly yourself, the favor and learn from this - ease up on exclusives and seize the potential cash cow that is pc gamers ;)

Where to even start with this game. I won't add spoilers, but even though the gameplay is great, and the graphics are top notch, it's the story that really hooks me and makes me think about the game even after having beat it several times. 

To say that Horizons story is epic is like saying The Matrix was cool. It's an understatement. I've played a lot of games, and it is difficult to surprise me with plot, story, voice acting, motion capture. After hundreds of games, after awhile their stories start (rightly) looking like bad soap opera scripts, where the villain is as likely to monologue you to death as they are to fight you. Where you're forced to listen to endless manifestoes by the bad guys trying to justify their decisions. 

Horizon is not like that. While it's story is fantastical and unbelievable, it is also not a soap opera. It's dramatic, but not fake hollywood drama. The writing of this game is more on par with a Nebula Award wining scifi novel. The team that wrote this game should write a book because as a fervent scifi reader, I would have put this story up there with The Three Body Problem, with A Deepness in the Sky, with Children of Time, with The Diamond Age. It's that level of writing and world building and just wow. 

And the way the story unfolds, it's not forced exposition and narration that reveals the world of Horizons like a movie. Instead your own curiosity and need to know drives you to uncover the evidence, and to piece the puzzle together. Later in the game, much later, it is eventually made more clear what happened, but it never felt forced or boring. I never got the urge to skip a cutscene. 

The Acting. The people in the game, the voice actors, the animators, the directors, they managed to make the characters feel like living, breathing people, not like video game characters. When a character does something, when they befriend you, or fight you, they do so for reasons that make sense to them, not because the story demands they do those things. As such, you feel like these are real people, flawed, doing the best they can. Aloy especially is one of the greatest video game protagonists of the last 20 years. She is more badass than Master Chief and yet she isn't a slow walking away from an explosion badass, she's an approachable, grounded, empathetic hero that feels like a person trying to do actual good in the world, not some stick figure killing machine that action games usually use as a place holder for actual heroics. It is also refreshing to see a female character whos armor is not a string bikini and who has free agency in their life. Aloy doesn't have a B story where she falls in love, she's not wooed or wooing, she's not sexualized in any manner, and feels like something that video games could direly use more of. 

Then there are the NPCs in this world. Big, elaborate, organic, robo dinosaurs. You never get tired of seeing a walker the size of a skyscraper walk by and scaling it to get the lay of the land. Robo T-REX chasing you is the scariest thing in this game. Even when you can survive fighting them one on one, or learn the tame ability, encountering one of those things is always a heart attack. They just look so badass. I'm sure a real Trex never looked so incredibly deadly. 

I have become a jaded video game player, and I seldom get excited for games anymore, especially big budget AAA games that all look and feel the same, the repeat sequels every year, new far cry, new assassins creed, etc, so boring. But Horizon is THE best game I have played in the last 10 years at least. At least it's the most enjoyable game I've played in a very long time.

Here are some suggestions that I have gotten from other users that have helped me in the meantime for anyone that does have the game. As suggested by Steam User Jom, I put Shadows at low and Ambient Occlusion at medium (the lowest it can go without turning it off) while leaving other settings at high. This greatly reduced the amount of stuttering and hiccups that I got.

As suggested by Tiny Rick, I went into the game folder and ran the .exe in Admin mode. This is supposed to help prevent crashes. I've been out of the starting area for a while and am running around the world. There is still some pretty nasty pop-in that happens now and then, but I haven't had any crashes while doing this, and I tried upping my graphics to ultra. So far, no hitches that I've been able to see so far because of this. Will continue to test it out to see if it runs better.

Horizon Zero Dawn is a third person action game set in a post apocalyptic open world where the Earth has been overrun by machines and the remains of Humanity live in small tribes with primitive technology. The player character, Aloy, must go on a quest to investigate the origin of the machines and the fall of the previous civilization.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

•	Along her journey, Aloy will fight against machines and Human bandits. The design of the machines is really cool. Their appearance and behaviour is similar to animals such as horses, cows, tigers, bulls, crabs, crocodiles, hawks, or dinosaurs like the velociraptor, brontosaurus and t-rex. As well as melee attacks, some of them have laser weapons mounted on their back, or can spam fire or frost projectiles at you, and one machine even has a cloaking device.

•	Most bandits are armed with axe or bow, but their leaders have powerful heavy weapons like a minigun or grenade launcher, which you can pick up and use until they run out of ammo.

•	Aloy can wield a staff for melee attacks and various different types of bows which can shoot arrows enhanced with elemental damage. Fire does extra damage over time, frost will slow enemy movement and increase damage taken, while shock will stun them for a few seconds leaving them vulnerable to a critical melee attack. There’s also a really useful skill which lets you load up two or three arrows to fire simultaneously with any bow.

•	There’s a strong focus on using stealth, hiding in long grass to sneak past groups of powerful enemies, or getting close enough to perform a melee takedown on weaker enemies.

•	Combat can be quite tactical. One of my favourite weapons, the Tripcaster, lets you place explosive or shock tripwires on the ground, which will detonate when a machine runs over them. Before the start of a fight, I liked to place a few tripwires in strategic locations, between trees or rocks, then I’d stand with the tripwires between myself and the machines, shooting the machines with arrows while trying to lure them into charging through the tripwires.

•	Some machines have weak points that can be targeted to deal extra damage, or you can destroy their weapon components to reduce their threat to you, although this can be tricky when fighting against fast moving or flying enemies. Its actually easier when fighting bosses because of their huge size and slower movement.

•	You can unlock the ability to override machines to make them fight each other, or to use them as a mount to travel around the world quicker. I didn’t use mounts often because I quickly discovered that this will draw aggro from lots of nearby enemies (similar to driving a car in a Far Cry game), so its less stressful to just sneak around on foot.

•	You can buy several outfits from traders which change Aloy’s appearance. Weapons and outfits can be upgraded with modifications which provide bonuses to various damage types, damage resistances, or stealth.

[h1]Story[/h1]

•	Story is very well written with an interesting sense of mystery, and I enjoyed slowly piecing together what happened in the old world. The conflict between Humans and machines has similarities to the likes of The Terminator and The Matrix.

•	Most side quests have unique stories which are of a similar quality level to those in Witcher 3, and much better than the copy and paste tasks usually found in open world games. Sometimes you’ll wander across machines and Humans fighting each other, while clearing bandit camps will allow friendly tribes to move in. All of these elements help to bring the world to life.

•	Voice acting is fantastic, especially Ashly Burch (who previously voiced Chloe in Life is Strange) as Aloy and Lance Reddick (Fringe, Quantum Break) who plays an important supporting character.

•	Lip syncing during cutscenes is the best I’ve seen since Hellblade Senua’s Sacrifice.

[h1]Technical[/h1]

•	The environment looks fantastic, from the forests, rivers and snowy mountains to deserts and ruined buildings of the old world.

•	I had a smooth framerate during combat with machines and while exploring the world. The only significant problems I encountered were around a few bandit camps where my framerate dipped into the 40s, I’m assuming this was caused by columns of smoke because I didn’t see them anywhere else. I had some minor framerate drops in large settlements of NPCs, which wasn’t the end of the world because it didn’t affect any fast paced gameplay.

•	It took me 61 hours to complete the main quest, expansion, and lots of side quests. During this time I only crashed twice, so the game was very stable for me. Both crashes occurred before the release of patch 1.06 so it seems that whatever was causing the problem has been fixed.

•	Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.

•	The camera has a mind of its own, sometimes changing position by itself. By default, Aloy will be slightly offset to the left of screen, like most third person games. However, there are times when the camera drifts so that Aloy is almost all the way to the right of the screen, which feels slightly disorienting. Its not an issue that makes the game unplayable, because you can immediately reset the camera position by aiming the bow. This also means its not a problem during combat because you’ll almost always be aiming. Its just a really strange design decision that doesn’t serve any purpose, and I can’t think of any other game I’ve played in the last few years where I’ve felt like I’m fighting the camera.

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

Horizon Zero Dawn is an amazing game and I rate it as an absolute must play for action game fans. Combat and story are both excellent and while there are some technical flaws, they aren’t big enough reasons to avoid playing. The amount of content makes this easily worth a full price purchase.

Where should I even start..

I bought Horizon Zero Dawn after months of wishlisting it. I liked how it looked, I liked the setting, but I didn't expect anything phenomenal - oh, I was so wrong.

This game takes you on an emotional rollercoaster. At so many points in the game, I thought I had figured the story out and I was wrong every single time. This game never stopped surprisng me.
How each cutscene digs you deeper into the story of Horizon Zero Dawn is fantastic. It's beautiful, it's hopeful, it's gut wrenching, it's devestating - and I loved every bit of it.

The world itself is also a joy to explore and walk through. Just as beautiful as the story itself.

This is a game I would've gotten for $60 if I had known how good it is and I normally wait for sales on games.
I recommend buying this game at quite literally any price you'll ever see on Steam, but there are regular sales. I got it for around $17.

I've seen people scoff at the comparison, but Horizon Zero Dawn has a lot in common with later Assassin's Creed entries. If you're no fan of those, you [i]probably[/i] won't like this game either - at least from a pure gameplay perspective.

[b]However[/b]; I found the world building, stories and quests are a lot more fleshed out here. The main campaign is great, the map is efficient, and although there's grinding to be had, it's negligible. If you do run out of resources, it's never far away.

Also, having played both the PS4 version and now PC - bow hunting with KB/M and the precision it gives, is the far superior way to play the game. It almost made the game trivial, even on the hardest difficulty.

Having just finished a playthrough on Ultra Hard New Game+, earning the last few achievements I was missing, I feel now is the time to write a review for this game. And, as it usually happens after I finished a game that got me so involved, I find it hard to start the review.

So, Horizon Zero Dawn. The first PlayStation first-party game to ever release on PC. Back when it was first announced, I was beyond excited, it was a dream come true, not just because of this game, but because of potential future Sony releases on PC. However, we aren't talking about that here, we're talking about HZD. So I bought it when it was available, started it up when it released... And ended up abandoning it for years, until last year, when I finally got back to it, and it finally "clicked".

First things first, let's talk story and lore. The game takes place in a post-apocalyptic Earth, where humanity has regressed to a more tribal civilization, after some unknown catastrophe devastated cities and left beast-like machines roaming the Earth. You play as Aloy, a young girl from the Nora tribe, who has been an outcast her entire life; even then, she's allowed to win back her place in the tribe by taking part of the Proving, but, of course... Things happen, and Aloy gets thrown in the middle of a conflict that could bring down not only her tribe, but all of civilization itself. On top of that, Aloy is searching for answers about her past. The story is very good, but I must say where the game really shines is with the lore; although saying more about it would spoil the fun of discovering it as you progress to the game.

As for gameplay, it's an open world game, with the typical stuff you'd expect from such a game. Main quests, side quests, collectibles, upgrades and so on and so forth. The first time I tried playing the game, it didn't quite click with me because I wasn't using the full extent of what the game offers, and thus, the combat felt somewhat frustrating (I was only ever using the default bow). There's actually a decent variety of weapons to use, and even for bows there's actually three main variants: one focused on what I'd call "general" damage, one for elemental effects, and a more specialized one for specific situations. On top of the bows, you can get a bomb slingshot, set traps, tie machines down, plus a couple more weapons both from the main game and the DLC. You can also use stealth for certain encounters, and there's a wide variety of potions that can aid you in combat.

Enemy variety is pretty good. It's mostly machines, with some humans here and there, but you'll mostly fight machines. Another part of the combat I didn't quite get at first was how to deal with machines; not just which weapons to use, but how to exploit their weaknesses. For example, some machines might have fuel canisters on them; you can set them off with a fire weapon to cause an explosion dealing area damage, stuff like that. Other machines might be able to detect you while you're hiding, until you destroy their sensors, leaving them blind; well, not really blind, as they can still see you, but they can't find you as easily if they lose sight of you.

I enjoyed exploring in this game; the world they've crafted is beautiful. There are some headscratching parts (like going from snowy mountains to a hot desert), but I chalk that up to games being games; making the trek from one region to the other more realistic would mean a lot of pointless travelling, so distances are shortened. Anyway, the game has some really beautiful locations, even more so the DLC region, which has a volcano looming in the background.

Speaking of the DLC, I enjoyed it as much as the main game, although I gotta say, I'm not sure if I'll ever go through it in NG+. It's certainly way more challenging than the base game, with some new machines that can deal quite some damage. Its story connects with that of the main game, and you can even get some more info about a certain character through the DLC.

Which brings me to the characters: I liked most of them, except one whom I particularly despise for what he caused; I'm not going to talk further than that as it'd be spoilers, but I'm sure you'll know which character I'm talking about after you get through the game. Anyway, going back at it, the game has a diverse cast of characters; each tribe has its own customs that you learn throughout the story. The dialogue, I found very good, and some of Aloy's interactions with certain characters were really funny.

Visually, the game looks stunning. I noticed some details here and there, but that was probably because I played it in medium settings. In higher settings it'd probably look even better. The soundtrack is also very good.

I definitely recommend this game, it certainly became one of my favourite "new" franchises, and I can't wait to play Forbidden West next.

If you've ever wanted to blow up giant robot dinosaur things with primitive weaponry, this is probably the game for you.

Simply an amazing game. The storyline is intriguing enough to make you want to follow it, and the world itself is full enough that aimlessly wandering through it is fun and often satisfying in its own rite. The variety of weapons allows you to cater much of the game to your play style, whether you prefer to sneak and snipe, run in with guns (or, I guess, arrows) blazing, or use traps to ambush your enemies (although you'll probably do all that and more).

There are several human bandit types that you'll need to kill, but for the most part you'll be fighting various machines, mostly designed with inspiration from the animal kingdom. Horizon Zero Dawn (HZD) has a very whimsical, yet interesting concept that can be boiled down to: local cave-woman fight robotic dinosaurs in a destroyed world. Does this open-world product live up to its premise? Let's dive in.
 
[h2]Pros[/h2]
- A beautiful, destroyed world 
- Unforgettable post-apocalyptic story 
- Huge variety of enemies
- Brilliant combat system
- Tons of entertaining side activities

[h2]Cons[/h2]
- Choices presented are mostly meaningless

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Graphics-wise, this is a damn gorgeous piece of art, which is to be expected from a former Playstation exclusive title. The world feels alive with its alluring scenery and vibrant color palette. With different biomes available to traverse, you will never get bored of exploring. I highly recommended turning off the HUD elements for maximum immersion.

HZD follows a similar structure to most open-world games, being a large sandbox with plenty of fun distractions. Of course, the main activity lies within fighting the machines with the game’s excellent combat system. With more than 20 types of enemies to fight against, each one has its unique behaviors and weaknesses that you can exploit. For instance, machines that detect your position can be prevented by destroying their tracking component while large opponents have mounted ranged weapons that you can detach and use against them. 

Moreover, you are given a plethora of deadly tools to fight the machines. Starting with the humble but versatile basic bow, new equipment and more powerful variants of the previous ones will be available as you steadily level up such as the ropecaster (tie-up enemies) and tearblaster (rip components off). Even the bow comes in three distinct types and nine unique arrows. 

Fighting robots is not the only source of fun here. Tons of optional side content is provided for you to enjoy. Thirsty for human blood? Liberate a bandit camp. Want to challenge and time yourself? Go to a Hunting Ground. Desire to help people? Do errands for them. There is no shortage of quests available for you to tackle. Some of them even gives you special rewards that cannot be obtained through other methods.

Apart from that, management plays a big part in everything you do as inventory is limited. Resources come in many shapes and sizes, and if you have too much, you have to sell some of them. Crafting ammo is something you will be doing frequently, and the more powerful ones require costs more to make. Thankfully, the game is pretty generous in providing you loot that can be scavenged from fallen machines, humans and the occasional ancient debris. 

[h1]Story[/h1]
In an unfamiliar time, the world has seemingly been plunged into darkness. Humans, while still existing, now live as primitive tribes with distinctive customs and beliefs. To make matters worse (or confusing), the unkempt wilds are filled with animal-like machines of unknown origins that are hostile to mankind. You are Aloy, a woman that was born outside the tribe as an outcast. As she is treated as a freak of nature by her tribe due to not having a mother, her only friend is his surrogate father, Rost. Being taught how to survive physically and emotionally by him, Aloy embarks on a thrilling adventure across the lands to find the truth behind her existence, and potentially change the world in the process.

HZD does a magnificent job of introducing you to the game’s premise without being too overwhelming. The world-building trickled out slowly at first but gradually expands as you progress through the storyline. Besides that, it is also thick with lore thanks to the enormous amounts of story collectibles that shed light on the world that came before. For the most part, it did fairly well in balancing between a ‘chosen one’ plot and a coming-of-age story for Aloy.

Unfortunately, the game’s ‘choices system’ falls flat on its face. While you are given three choices at certain points (to be sympathetic, smart, or cruel), it does nothing of value apart from barely changing a few lines of dialogue. The story beats remain the same with a single ending. Sometimes, you can decide to spare or kill certain characters, but even those have little to no repercussions towards Aloy’s journey. 

[b]The Rest[/b]
[list]
[*] Every machine usually has one of the following major weaknesses: fire (deals continuous damage), freeze (slows movement and amplifies damage), and electric (stuns enemies). 
[*] Most weapons and outfits can be equipped with modifications to increase their effectiveness. The higher the gear level, the more slots you have.
[*] Wild animals can be found and hunted for their meat, skin, and bone. These are used to craft health potions or to expand your inventory. 
[*] After a certain point, you will gain the ability to ride certain machines as mounts. They are an excellent way to travel the world quickly without fast travel. 
[*] Leveling up gives you one skill point that can be used in the skill tree. Some are basic upgrades like faster reloading while others are game-changing such as the ability to perform silent kills.
[/list]

[h1]Stats[/h1]
[b]Playtime:[/b] It took me around 90 hours to complete the base game on Normal difficulty and an additional 20 hours for the DLC.

[b]Replayability:[/b] Very much so, especially if you are interested in the grueling Ultra Hard difficulty as picking that option significantly changes the mechanics and enemy AI.

[b]Achievements:[/b] 79 of them. Most of them can be earned simply by doing quests and the optional stuff.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
HZD is a shining example of triple A game done right. The world is mesmerizing, the gameplay is solid, and the storyline is enjoyable. For me, the highlight is the combat system; easy to learn yet hard to master. Therefore, I recommend Horizon Zero Dawn.

A superb game. There are a few minor negatives, discussed below, but positives include:

* An thoughtful story, revealed perfectly through the game's events. The strongest part of the game is archaeologically uncovering text, audio, and holograms that gradually reveal the past and fill out the daily lives of the Old Ones and what happened to them.
* Absolutely stunning world design. Varied and realistic natural biomes, artfully distressed artifacts such as broken-down satellite dishes, ruined buildings reclaimed by plant life, and two styles of advanced architecture: near-future ruins of the Old Ones, and contemporary machine-built spaces built with a tetrahedral theme.
* Good voice acting (with a few exceptions), particularly Lance Reddick in the role of Sylens.
* A true female protagonist: tart, sarcastic, and even a little unlikable at times. A deep character that happens to be female, not eye candy and not sexualized, with understandable motivations and reactions.
* Well-integrated DLC that is aware of your progression through the main story and vice versa. Frozen Wilds is a meaningful expansion to the plot and includes some of the better voice acting in the game. A personal favorite is the opportunity to have quite a lot of dialog with the AI at the core of the DLC plot after you've completed it.
* Fun, frantic, and difficult combat with robots (at least on my initial playthrough on 'hard'). The game really makes you engage with the elemental effect and localized damage systems in order to be successful. Stealth is possible but in sort of a Dishonored way where you use stealth while you can and then its time to rock and roll.
* A good port. I found it quite playable with mouse and keyboard and had no crashes or noticeable technical issues in a 70 hour completion run.

Minor negatives that detract a little from the experience:

* A lot of systems seem a little half-baked. For instance climbing is only possible on specially-marked ledges, and there is no gameplay challenge or puzzle element, you just bounce from ledge to ledge. Likewise you can see some thought put into restricting fast travel via limited craftable travel supplies, but in practice those supplies are so abundant that you can fast travel whenever. There are some other examples of what I can only guess is cut content or studio fluff.
* Some cringey voice acting among minor characters and dialog on side missions. Side missions often devolve down to a go-here-and-follow-tracks procedure which is tedious when repeated several times.
* In general the game is dumbed down a bit and the path to progression is strongly hinted, or sometimes even outright told to you out loud. The few 'puzzles' are trivial and there's really no challenge to discovery.
* The archaeological digging around, which again is the most compelling part of the game, is for the most part confined to the main quest. Exiting the tutorial I had the expectation that there would be various caves and old installations to explore in the manner of Fallout, but unfortunately that is not really the case.

Overall an easy recommendation, especially on sale. Looking forward to the port of the sequel! #pcmasterrace

Horizon Zero Dawn is, for the most part, a solid, middle-of-the-road, generic open-world action-adventure game. It is perfectly competent in basically all areas, but doesn't really do much to innovate or stand out from the extremely crowded, extremely saturated field of generic open-world action-adventure games. Thankfully, it is saved by its one actual innovation: fighting giant robot animals using bows.

HZD does an excellent job of making the robots feel threatening and dangerous at every stage of the game, no matter how high your level or how powerful your equipment, while still making them feel like surmountable challenges that can be overcome with tactics and cunning. Obviously, blindly firing arrows at robots will do next to nothing, even with the best bows in the game, and you will find yourself getting smacked around like a giant cat toy. First, you will need to scan a new robot type while staying hidden to learn where all their weak points are, whether it be optic cameras, batteries or fuel canisters. Often, these parts will be protected by armour plating, which you will have to first remove by shooting them with armour-stripping arrows. Then, you will need to shoot at the exposed area to deal critical damage to the robot. If you use the correct ammo type, such as flaming arrows for fuel canisters or electrified arrows for batteries, you can cause elemental explosions which will damage all nearby robots, which will be useful if you are hunting multiple robots at once. If you are able to ambush a robot, you might be able to set up tripwires ahead of time to damage or stun robots. If a robot is too mobile to deal with, you can use harpoon ropes to anchor them to the spot. In all scenarios, there is always an element of strategy and finesse when hunting robots, and you never feel like you're trivialising the game with sheer firepower. Every encounter with a robot, even when doing mundane things like farming components for weapon upgrades, feels fun and exciting.

If there's one thing to criticise about the bow combat system, it's the lack of evolution in weapons as the game progresses. Very early on in the game, you gain the ability to craft the starter form of every ranged weapon in the game: three different types of bow, crossbow, slingshot etc. At that point, you basically have every combat option you will get in the game. You can get upgraded bows which deal more damage and can use more elemental arrows, but 90% of using elemental arrows is just "shoot arrow type A at weakpoint type A," so your experience in using these weapons basically remains unchanged for the entire game. This is alleviated somewhat in the DLC story, which allows you to unlock 4 new weapon types that function completely differently than your other weapons, but the DLC is targeted at a pretty high level, so you will still go through most of the game with the same few weapons.

As for why there are highly advanced robot animals in a post-apocalyptic world of primitive humans in the first place, HZD does a surprisingly excellent job with its plot and worldbuilding. The story of HZD is well-written and well-paced, first starting small with the protagonist Aloy wondering about her mysterious origins and trying to save her tribe, then gradually expanding to learning about the origins of the current state of the world they live in and trying to save the entire world. The game could have very easily shrugged its shoulders and said "we're giving you freaking ROBOT DINOSAURS with freaking LASER BEAMS on their heads, are you really going to question where they came from" and most people would have been perfectly understanding, but instead they chose to craft a rich, believable setting in which to populate all manner of mechanical beasts.

However, while the plot of the game is consistently good throughout, the same cannot be said for the character writing. Thankfully, the important characters are all done well: father figure is fatherly, mysterious ally is mysterious, antagonist is a constant insufferable dick, and Aloy herself is a sympathetic protagonist. However, almost every other NPC in the game is a flat cardboard sign meant to point you towards your next objective and disappear forever. This is the kind of game story that you will find more fun diving into in a fan wiki than actually playing reading about in game.

Unfortunately, that is where the accolades for this game end. Everything else in HZD is painfully generic open-world filler content. You got your three fighting styles of ranged, melee and stealth, where melee and stealth are painfully underbaked compared to the game's bow combat. You got your bandit camps scattered around the map to liberate, populated entirely by human enemies, which are so much more boring to fight compared to robot sabertooth tigers. You got your Uncharted-style traversal system, where you can only climb on special yellow-coloured rocks and ledges and it's really just a glorified linear path, which feels so dated and restricted now that we've experienced BotW's freeform stamina-based climbing system. You even have grinding random forest critters to farm drops to craft new weapons, which feels so extremely lame and out-of-place when compared to hunting down a giant robot crocodile to extract a machine core. It feels like a lot of these were added to the game because they couldn't think of anything better to pad the game out with and they decided to go with what everyone else is doing, instead of truly making design decisions to support a truly wonderful core gameplay hook of hunting bus-sized killer machines with caveman tools.

Overall, Horizon Zero Dawn is a good game. I don't want my criticisms of it to detract from that fact. However, it is certainly not the second coming of Jesus that the hype surrounding the game would have you believe. Everything that makes this game unique is a truly shining experience, but unfortunately everything else is painfully generic and fails to help the good stuff reach its full potential.

Horizon Zero Dawn is a post-apocalyptic open-world RPG where you kill a bunch of machines and evil henchmen on your way to saving what remains of humanity.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]The graphics are beautiful.
[*]The story line is fairly decent and has a very unique setting.
[*]There is a fairly in-depth and explained historical background for the setting (though it requires some suspension of disbelief as it uses fantasy science).
[*]It has an interesting and versatile combat system that is easy to pick up and difficult to master.
[*]There is minimal to no grinding required.
[*]It truly is an open-world game as you can basically go everywhere with minimal story line progression required.
[/list]

[h1]Neutral:[/h1]
[list]
[*]I honestly cannot recall the background music for this game. So it clearly was not particularly memorable (neither for good nor bad reasons).
[*]Available array of weapons was pretty bland and uninteresting. Upgrades/customization of said weaponry was also just unexciting (though still useful).
[*]The DLC was not particularly interesting (more of the same stuff) but it did come with some new weapons, armor, and powerful new versions of existing weapons.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]The characters are rather boring - I honestly did not find any of the actual characters to be interesting and instead was more intrigued by the dead historical characters.
[*]The combat grows stale after a while (like 20-30 hours in, combat was more of a chore than anything particularly difficult or interesting).
[*]While this game is an RPG... it only fits that category very very loosely. The choices presented to the main character are basically inconsequential.
[*]Side quests are repetitive, boring, unoriginal, and any other synonyms of the aforementioned.
[*]Mounts are seriously limited and suck. With so many cool machines, you are limited to three very banal mounts (and none of them can fly).
[*]Achievements require you to beat NG+, which is literally the same thing as NG except with better weapons available. Moreover, one of the achievements requires you to beat it on Ultra Hard (regardless of if you had beaten NG on Ultra Hard), making it even more of a chore.
[/list]

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]
Horizon Zero Dawn is a good game. I would be lying if I said that this game was anything spectacular, however I would also be lying if I did not admit that this game was a pretty fun journey overall. I recommend playing this game casually and at a reasonably quick pace rather than trying to do everything available (as the game will quickly feel repetitive after 20-30 hours). Essentially, if you play HZD at a casual pace while focusing primarily on the story, it is actually a really enjoyable adventure. However, if you try to finish everything (e.g. all achievements), the game will feel like a slow grind. I would 100% recommend getting this game if it goes on sale. Otherwise, you may want to consider what you are looking for in a game before you spend $50 on HZD.

I bought this game on PS4 originally when it came out, and had a great time playing it. Since then, Sony has shifted focus to putting their original exclusive titles on PC after launch.

This game in particular has had a bumpy start with hardware compatibility issues, however it's worth noting that they have patched 4 times already since launch, and the game is more stable and better performing each time.

On my particular hardware setup, the game runs very smoothly. I have a relatively high end PC (9900k, 2070 S) but my friend who uses this game from my library (Yay steam sharing on this game!) has a lower end but very common PC (Some I7, GTX 1660) and it also runs great on his machine post updates! So for anyone who was worrying if the hardware was in the way, I think it's very safe to say most rigs now should be able to run without crashing or severe performance issues!

And outside of hardware, the game is a gem for the start of a series. It definitely has it's own issues, cheese dialogue, weird hand made facial animations (no mocap for realism) kind of gives it an uncanny valley feeling. These were just some of the issues with this being an original title and the developers only having so much time and budget.

But the gameplay is fantastic, killing and hunting giant robots is a blast regardless. They keep getting stronger, but so do you. And the main story is an interesting engagement with the idea of radicalized corporatism, letting companies and their technologies evolve to a point of no return. That idea isn't new on its own; however the way it's explored in Horizon: Zero Dawn is entirely unique. Worth a shot at any price, for open world lovers looking for a cool series to get involved in.

Happy hunting.

Horizon: Zero Dawn is the living proof that you can make a great game if you have a great story, great writer and great designers. People can and will overlook even the most crazy and frustrating decisions of the game, if you have a spark of greatness in your game. Horizon: Zero Dawn has many great moments and even greater frustrations. 

You will stay for two things in this game:
 
A) The visuals: Sometimes the visuals means artstyle, sometimes it means graphics. This time it means both. HZD is a beautiful game with great, realistic graphics, amazing models and great textures. The art style is also great. From snowy mountains to deserts, from the different types of machines, the cities and the plains,  everything feels alive in this game and you will be immersed from the first moment you'll play.

B) The story. And what a story it is. It's structurally a masterpiece. You'll focus on the story of Aloy, a young huntress who is determined to find out about her ancestry. Simple. In this quest you'll discover gradually that her story is bigger than she was expecting, and bit by bit you will uncover the bigger picture that fills the gap of the lore of the world, plus you will take down the evil cult that wants to kill you. It feels a bit generic, but it does many things right: 1) the main quest is memorable and it has a lot of "wow" moments. 2) Great characters: the villains are a bit underutilized but other characters like Aloy, Sylens, Rost, Erend shine like diamonds. 3) the lore of the world is exceptional and it feels engaging.

Still the game has A TON of bad choices that will frustrated you. I wanted several times to quit but my will to see the story, made me pull through: 

A) Over-aggro machines. I know it's intended, but it sucks in 2 major ways: First, the travelling of the world feels bad because you are constantly attacked by random packs of machines that roam the roads. So instead of going from A to B, you will be going from A to killing machines and from there to B. Secondly and most importantly, these over-aggro machines hinder your battle. Let's say you want to take out a big machine. You attack it but in doing so you alert EVERY machine in a radius of a hundred meters, so most of these battles end up in a clusterf@#$. 

B) Bad levelgating: In addition to the above, sometimes you will aggro enemies that are way above your level. I just wanted to kill some scrappers and more times than none I ended up dying to a thunderjaw. Or the other time that a quest was indicated as a level 20, and the enemy inside was level 27. 

C) Attrocious level tree: Level trees are about powering up and unlocking cool abilities, right? Well not in HZD. Here you will unlock the very basics like "stealth kill" or "have a mount". That's right. You have to spend 9 level points to just have a permanent mount. Or be able to strike from above. or to have more room in your inventory. Also Fast travel in this game is not free. You need resources or you will need to buy a certain item from a vendor.

D) Gear: The gear is bad because there is a small variety of it, just a couple of weapons and armor in uncommon, rare and epic. Nor the machines nor the humans drop armor as a loot which is strange, but fine. The problem is that the armor is exclusively found in vendors, which are paid in both currency and in resources, so if you want to have a better armor (as I late found in the game) you have to start taking hunting seriously. 

E) Some bad combat mechanics; First the big machines (like thunderjaws and behemoths) are calibrated badly. They are huge, do a ton of damage, but also are insanely fast, like you can never outrun them in a battle and  they can reach you in just a jump. Actually their animations are so fast, that even with the time-slow movement you will often miss because they move faster than the projectile. 

Still HZD is great game despite the flaws I find. And I believe that this shows how great a game must be, if I am willing to overlook all these flaws that could be easily be avoided.

[h1] ♦️ Horizon Zero Dawn [/h1]
[b] Horizon Zero Dawn [/b] is one of Sony’s few first party IPs to make its way to PC and the Steam platform. For years throughout the Ps4s lifecycle we heard critics and fans alike rave about Horizon and what an experience it is. Now we get to test their claims at a high resolution with unlocked framerates.

[h1] Story & Characters [/h1]
[h3] Narrative [/h3]
→ Horizon starts off by giving us a taste at this strange new world. The feelings of excitement and awe during my first couple hours were at an all time high. Part of the story is fully grasping and immersing yourself in Horizons bizarre world. The narrative is a relatively basic one, and takes a little while to get up to speed. But once it does get the ball rolling it really starts laying the real truth behind Aloys past and how this future of Earth came to be. 
→ Aloy is on a mission to find out her true purpose, all while this strange corruption is plaguing machines and wreaking havoc among Earth's remaining population.I won’t go into detail but the second half of the game really starts answering questions about the truth of this world. Horizon’s story is a really exciting journey from start to finish, filled with enough twists and turns to keep you at the edge of your seat.
 
[h3] Characters [/h3]
→ Through the roughly ~40 hour campaign you will learn with Aloy about her past and fall in love with her as a person. Aloy is an amazing protagonist who reacts believably to shocking events. And through the journey you will come across supporting characters some good, some bad, some outright mysterious. Each and every one of them play a big role one way or another to progression Aloy to her goals. All have their own personal goals and missions with a unique personality
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2190824098

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
[h3] Combat [/h3]
→ The main form of fighting off these ferocious machines is through meleeing with your spear or shooting one of dozens of projectiles. Aloys hits make an impacting clash as her weapons clang off monstrous machines. And retreating back with a bow is always a viable strategy if that is more your jist. If you want an idea of how the combat plays it’s similar to how Monster Hunter: World feels, where you must use all tools at your disposal to take down gigantic beasts. The machines attacked are heavily choreographed and require you to learn attack patterns for almost every machine. And pressing ‘v’ to turn on your focus will highlight weak points and show weaknesses for whichever machine you highlight. This turns combat into this fast paced in and out game where you strike with your spear, dodge, and try to fire at its weak points with your bow. 
→ Aloy also has a roll to dodge enemy attacks which is difficult to master but is necessary to take on some of the biggest machines: There is also a stealth option to get the first strike on unsuspecting machines, and useful for taking out camps of humanoids Metal Gear Solid style.

[h3] Difficulty [/h3]
→ Horizon offers six different difficulty settings ranging from ‘Story’ to ‘Ultra Hard’ depending if you just want to focus on the story or if you want to stay awake at night in fear of saw-toothed robotic pumas. I played on ‘normal’ and I feel it gave a great experience, where combat was hard enough to make me focus but wasn’t easy enough to zone out and just wait for the next cutscene to play.

[h3] Weapons & Tools [/h3]
→ You have your usual bow, bigger bow, and spear but unique weapons like the tripcaster, sling, or rope gun. Your bow can of course be equipped with many different status ailments for use depending on the enemies weakness. This can be from fire arrows to armor piercing ones. And the tripcaster can lay status ailment lines that cause damage when enemies walk through them. The ropecaster can pin enemies to the ground leaving them vulnerable to heavy damage. Horizon offers many types of enemies to battle with more than enough different ways to defeat them, and no option is more right than any other.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2193009924

[h3] Upgrades [/h3]
→ Throughout your journey you will come across merchants that will trade you new armors and weapons in return for your resources. This provides incentive to kill machines to get all their drops as many machines provide an individual ‘currency’ to trade for unique armors and weapons. You’re also given the option to craft upgrades to your ammo pouches, carrying capacity on health potions. Etc. Meanwhile you will get modifications from defeated enemies that can be slotted in your armor and weapons for powerful buffs. This can be from +armor piercing to better handling.

[h3] Skills [/h3]
→ Not only are you tailoring your gear and weapons best suited for your playstyle, you also gain skill points on leveling up to enhance certain aspects of Aloy. If you want to rely heavily on your bow then upgrade its ‘slow-mo’ time and learn how to fire three arrows at once. If you want to be up close and personal enhance your weapon damage with deadly finisher attacks.

[h3] Enemy Design [/h3]
→ One of Horizons many eye catching design choices, is of course the various machines you will encounter. I can say that each machine fights differently with their own fighting styles. With over twenty plus different enemies you will encounter, each being as thrilling as the other. Think of each enemy as a sort of Dark Souls [i](Are we still comparing games to Dark Souls in 2020?)[/i] boss where they each have an attack pattern to learn and large attacks to avoid.

[h3] Side Content [/h3]
→ Besides the main story there is a load of side content to get lost in. From interesting side missions with their own little arc and of course uninteresting fetch quests. Also including exploring ‘ruins’ to gain important knowledge on certain enemy types. It even has timed trials if that is more of your thing. Most importantly Horizon on PC comes with a whole extra fifteen hours of story in the form of its expansion “Frozen Wilds”.

[h1] Visuals & Sound [/h1]
[h3] Visuals [/h3]
→  The world design rivals Red Dead 2s visual quality. Filled with high quality textures with an amazing day/night cycle that brings in otherworldly lighting effects. There were many points across my playthrough where I had to take a good minute and pause in photo mode to admire the visual fidelity offered by Gorilla Games. I will say that at the launch of Horizon on PC performance was quite rocky and my 1080ti struggled to get playable frame rates and constantly crash. But I have played Horizon recently with my 1080ti and I will say the many patches made, it is finally at a really acceptable level of port quality.

[h3] Sound [/h3]
→ To accompany the amazing visual design there is also an impressive sound design. Each enemy sounds viscous in its own right, their attacks crack with explosions and really sound scary. And on the opposite end there is blissful music that pairs perfectly with Horizons stunning vistas. The music is a combination of free flowing beats with robotic sounds spiking at times, it really sells this prehistoric yet futuristic world of Horizon Zero Dawn.

Horizon Zero Dawn is a phenomenal game with a captivating story, breathtaking visuals, well-designed and extremely fun combat with magnificent machines, likeable friendly cast of characters and some dull villains.


The story is a tale of the ones who came before and how the current world came to be. Although it is not an entirely fresh take, it is very engaging as Aloy learns about what was, progresses and grows in terms of knowledge and capabilities. It is filled with intriguing events, charming conversations and is an emotional journey as Aloy learns who she is in this new world. There are hundreds of audio notes and texts to read, the story is often expanded upon via them.

Aloy's performance is excellent throughout the story. She's sarcastic, funny, compassionate, smart and can even be aggressive if you want to go that route. She's cocky at times but is capable enough to pull off even the difficult of tasks. 

The world in this game is a sight to behold, it is simply beautiful. The closest I can compare it to is The 100 show's setting. The open-world is filled with many activities to do, which may get repetitive but features compelling side missions with smaller archs.

Combat is the best part of this game featuring various types of ranged weapons with many kinds of ammunition types. There are different types of bows as well, from fast shooting of arrows to long-ranged slow shots. Features 4 weapon slots only. Skill system is good with worthwhile upgrades. Enemy machine design is smart with various attacks but have weaknesses to exploit. 

Boss fights are decent, can be as easy or difficult as you want them to be. There are various difficulty options, hard might be the sweet spot without being overly punishing. Climbing mechanics are fluid.

Some of the cutscenes are pre-rendered but are of high quality. Aloy's companions or the friends she makes are characters with good backstory. Some of them have their own side-quests. Human enemies are lacking depth and may feel one-dimensional, especially one of the main villains. 

Soundtrack gives you chills, it is wonderful and epic. 

Performance on PC is good, with a great implementation of DLSS and has FSR support. A console-equivalent preset is provided for the same level of visual fidelity. Keyboard controls were not an issue and the dynamic HUD was very welcomed.

The price of this title was increased by three times over in some regions and I do not see nor can't think of any logical explanation except for the publisher being greedy. The initial regional pricing was very appreciated and it stayed like that for around two years. If this is the behaviour publishers are going for, they will be hurting their own sales. Disappointing and unacceptable, such a shame.

Zero Dawn is a worthwhile experience even for its increased price tag and an amazing achievement by Guerrilla. Hopefully the sequel arrives sooner on PC than expected.

[h1]Earth is ours no more[/h1]

2020 has been quite a year for video-games, we got a new Half-Life entry, a Persona game launched on PC since 1996 and we got the announcement of a Sony’s 1st Party flagship coming to PC, Horizon Zero Dawn. Truth be told, it’s not the first Sony exclusive game to come to Steam, we also got the Quantic Dream games and recently Death Stranding but none published by themselves, now Horizon is a completely different case, it’s their first published game on Steam and who knows, maybe the first of many, anyway, the day has come and it’s time to review this adventure, so let’s find out if it’s worthy, shall we? 

Horizon Zero Dawn takes place in a distant future in which civilization has returned to the tribal era, the world has returned to a natural state and it’s populated by mechanical beasts, the machines. We play as Aloy, an outcast girl who wants to discover who’s her mother and why she is an outcast, her quest for the truth will lead Aloy into something much bigger that involves what happened to the world in the past and what’s happening between the tribes in the present. What happened to our world? That’s something we will find out. 

The story is really interesting, it gives you two perspectives, the first one is the present tribal time in which we will see how the society works in such conditions. Religious vision, political movements, social behaviours, all those elements will be present all the way until the end of our adventure. 
The Second perspective is the past, what happened to the world, why there are cities in ruins, why there are machines ruling the lands and not only big things but also we will see little fragments of the daily life of that society via documents, holograms and audio logs, don’t miss them, some are really good and there’s a lot of background content in this optional files. 

As the story is divided in two main arcs with their own mission timeline and both can be merged due to the freedom of choice when it comes to choose what mission you want to do I think I should give an advice about how I think it’s the best way of experimenting the story, the first arc you should do is the one that it’s about the present ([spoiler]Eren’s mission line[/spoiler]) until the end of it and then go all-in to the arc that it’s about the past ([spoiler]Orlin’s mission line[/spoiler]) as this will lead to the end and by how it is structured in terms of dialogues and choices, I think this makes more sense, the frozen wilds should be experimented after the main story for the same reason, dialogues and references make more sense. 

Game has a lot of side-quests, they provide a good chunk of exposition about more details of the present and there are some worthy characters that will be found in this side-activities (hunting grounds, infected zones, etc), make no mistake, not everything is worth it and the map is full of marks, while it’s not difficult to complete the side objectives, it is time consuming and maybe it’s not something you want to do, if you want to focus on the important ones, follow the green exclamation marks once you discover them, there are side-stories that are really interesting.

Side-activities will unlock more points to get more abilities and get better parts to get better gear, it’s not something mandatory but I think it’s enjoyable thanks to the gameplay.

Speaking of gameplay, there’s a lot to discuss here, let’s see, base gameplay is what you would expect from a third person action/adventure game, everything is as standard as you can imagine, however, it works really well, climbing is guided but very fluid,combat is functional, etc... however the only playable system that feels strange compared to other similar games is riding the machines, it feels clunky and I guess they wanted to make it feel heavy because, well, you are riding a mechanical horse and not an organic animal but I don’t think it makes you feel that but that it’s a non-functional riding.

Now returning to the combat there’s this thing that makes it something stunning, machine hunting. Combat against humans is the standard, melee and distance attacks, however their actions make them predictable so it’s easy to win their encounters, machines tho, while predictable they offer a much higher challenge in combat and it’s spectacular and a big part of what makes this game something unique, if there’s titanic beings combat in it, there’s already something special. 

Thunderjaw’s first combat is something remarkable. 

There’s no better way than that combat to introduce the graphics as yes, both the Thunderjaw and Horizon Zero Dawn are juggernauts, but a different kind of juggernaut, one is an alpha predator in the game and the other is top tier in terms of visual quality. 

HZD is probably one of the best looking games out there, a general look of the valley, the snowy mountains or the warm desert will make you say “woah” every single time you discover a new location, the lightning, the weather system, the forests and jungles and the ruins, everything looks absolutely fantastic, let’s keep in mind that this game came out in 2017, the fact that this can compete visually against more modern titles tells a lot in favor of this game, and not only in terms of world building but also in terms of character design, which is absolutely fantastic, aside of some weird animations from time to time when it’s time to talk, but overall it’s impossible to say this is not a good looking game and if you find it as one of the most beautiful games you have seen, well, I can feel you. 

Even the little details are present, sure, it’s not a world as reactive as we are used to see nowadays but 3 years can make a huge difference.
Make no mistake, there are rough textures, some weird invisible walls and a few other little things that will be there but overall, I don’t think you will notice.

What I’m sure you will notice is the sound design too because it’s really great and the most impressive part of it is the machine sounds, so industrial, so metallic, I love it. Human voices are also really great and well integrated. 

OST is really good, there are two or three themes that will stick with you for a long time, I’m sure. 

And now that I have more or less expressed my opinion about the general aspects of the game, I think it’s important to jump into the PC specifics, aka, the PC port. 

Horizon Zero Dawn launched in a very mixed state, while I had a really great experience in my system with no crashes or technical problems present during my adventure, I know I’m the exception and not the rule, in general a lot of people have been experiencing technical problems like stuttering or crashes and it’s something that must be acknowledged, even if you look for specific configurations performance there’s no warranty that it will run at the same quality as your installed programs might be interacting with the game too or some driver is different, I will say it pretty clear, while my experience was perfect I can’t assure you that you will have my same luck. 

However looking at the bright side, Guerrilla is doing a really great job communicating with users and fixing with patches all the problems they find, it’s Sony’s first game on PC so I will give you the benefit of the doubt and give them time to learn, at the very least, they have been quite active for the fixing and the communication, so that’s something great. 

And that’s pretty much it, my final thoughts is that this is an amazing game that will give you a lot of hours to explore and a really interesting story to follow, the machines are an absolutely main reason to get into this game. It still feels kind of surreal that we are able to play this on Steam but industry has changed a lot lately so anything is possible, I guess.

I just can say that I absolutely recommend this game and I surely hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

They ask for access to much more info than would be needed for a developer to help with troubleshooting or bug fixes for a single-player game. 

I looked around for justification and found none, so I felt that I had to conclude that the goal was to gather my (our) data simply to sell it...data that could possibly include identifying info and personal/private activities not related to the game. 

I'm aware that I'm already feeding my info to other nefarious companies, though that's mostly out of necessity to live and work in the modern world. It's plain depressing when those invasive fishhooks are embedded in our simple pleasures too. I'm personally uncomfortable allowing a business to pull that level of info from me when they have no use for it aside from selling it. 

It's a shame, but I've refunded the game and can't in good conscience recommend it while it sits behind this wall of telemetry. Same goes for any other games that follow the same profit-driven philosophy...data about your personal computer usage is not "trivial" or "useless" and don't let anyone tell you different.

Horizon Zero Dawn is an amazing adventure game where prehistoric meets futuristic.

Visually stunning with a story rich settled on an open world, it's quite astonishing what Guerrilla reached with it considering that at the time they developed it they still were just a game studio with few games released.

Aloy is a very charismatic character and while the story develops you learn with her what happened with this land based by robotic animals, a script that pretty much could set a sci-fi movie.

Rather than spin a story about naive tribes battling the evils of encroaching technology, this game had the gut to weave a tale that encompasses complex themes. A mature storytelling that we don't always see, it addresses abandonment issues, ethnic cleansing and touch on things we usually face as a modern society.

As far as the gameplay goes, it's pleasant how fluid it is, the mechanics of the combat are intuitive and at the same time it gives a healthy challange in which we cannot always relay on just one weapon through the whole game.

During the game you realize that sometimes it's best to switch your fighting style between stealh and agressive, you need to figure out how to beat each machine's attack pattern, capabilities and weaknesses to get a successful outcome without failing in the process or even dying. Extremely rewarding but progressivly tougher the longer you get into the storyline which in itself is very driven. 

The game offers us a large amount of side-missions, collectibles and challenges around the world to complete, if you are a completionist get ready to a deep run that will consume your time for several hours.

To wrap it up, very recommended. An exciting journey from the very start that leaves us with lots of interesting questions all while the development of Aloy as a person happens, what it means for her future trying to uncover the truths about this strange world. 
When most of them are finally answered there's yet much to come.

Worth mention that it came very chaotic to PC but nowadays it runs great, a good addition to your library if you like adventure games.

Oh, where to begin? I guess with a TLDR: This game is exceptional, it is worth playing and I think most gamers would agree with me. 

Now to the details! This game is a joy to behold, from the wonderful crafted ecosystems that feel real to the haunting and yet still beautiful soundtrack... Horizon: Zero Dawn does not disappoint. As you step into this world, an ice cold stream on one side and a field filled with swaying grass and deadly machines on the other, I hope you will be as captivated as I am. 

On the subject of those machines, they are equal parts awe inspiring and terrifying. Each has unique mechanics that make them all a very real threat, they force the player to adapt to the fight at hand or get squashed. They also all make sense, each filling a niche in the ecosystem and each playing a vital role in the new Earths future. 

Sure, there are some issues. The performance on PC isn't great if you don't have a very powerful PC and there are aspects of the game that are REALLY buggy. There's also a brutal difficulty curve if you want to 100% it as I have. But through these issues the core gameplay still shines for me. 

At the end of the day, is this game for everyone? Probably not. Is it worth everyone trying it at least once? YES. There's something here for most gamers. 10/10.

The story alone is worth the price of admission to me. Lots of mysteries get slowly uncovered as you progress. One scene in particular is a top 10 gaming story moment for me - I was holding my face in shock, I couldn't believe it.

Achievement hunters will also be pleased to hear that nothing in this game is missable. Every collectible, every achievement, every task -- you can backtrack later and do/get anything that you missed.

The combat is intuitive, though I wish there existed a faster spear attack. Sometimes it felt a little slow and clunky.

Graphics are gorgeous. Lots to explore, plenty to see. I was taking screenshot after screenshot because I kept encountering so many great views.

Really loved this game -- had a blast.

[h1]Horizon Zero Dawn[/h1]

First of all, don't get me wrong. It's a great game and well worth playing. Sony has managed to create one of the best and most memorable main characters in video game history. And certainly one of the the best female protagonist out there. Aloy is strong, intelligent, and kind. And has the right background to explain her epic skills in combat and survival. Not like some other female protagonist we all know. With abilities no human should have and that are never explained or those remembered mostly for their boobs.
But for this review, I will mainly focus on the game's bad side. And there's plenty of that in the game.

[b]Concept:[/b]

Let's tackle the elephant in the room. HZD uses the typical Ubisoft formula. They've used it so many times in Far Cry and their hundreds of Assassin's Creed games. Square used the same formula with the new Tomb Raider series and the Thief game. And now Sony used it with Horizon Zero Dawn. In itself it's nothing bad. But if you've played any of these games, you've pretty much seen it all. 
You have your main quest line, which takes around 5-6 hours if that's what you focus on mostly. And the rest is filled with all sorts of random things to artificially blow up playtime. Random loot you'll never really need unless you go on random animal and machine hunts, random vistas, random lore, random and repetitive side quests, random NPCs you'll never see again, random bandit camps, etc. That's a lot of random. It's enjoyable at first, but the more you play, you relize it just drags on and on and on. 
And all the random lore pieces in the world don't help at all. Because most of the time it's about something very trivial. No explanation about the world you live in or how the tribes build their things and their society, how the tribes themselves evolved so differently besides living so close to each other. It's a story telling mess and all over the place. So much potential lost.

So you have about 5-7 hours for the main quest and about 60-70 hours of random stuff. That's 10-15% on the essential and world building and the rest is just random. I'm pretty sure some people will like this kind of concept for some crazy reason, but when you think of some of the greatest games of all time, you just have to be disappointed. In these games you have the complete opposite. You have 80 percent and more time to grapple with the story, the concept, and all the little things about the world you're playing in, and the rest are things that don't matter that much to the bigger picture.

[b]Main story:[/b]

The main story is solid. Nothing new or unique. Nothing you haven't seen, read or heard. But it has a decent pacing, and just enough uniqueness to stand out from the rest. But there are no surprises and you will know everything in the middle of the main quest. Or even before that. Overall, the dialogues are not very well written and pretty basic at times.
That might sound a little harsh, but they ended up wasting 60 hours on random things instead of deepening the main story with a few more NPCs and lore. And it's not like the NPCs on the main path are very interesting either, apart from the main character and the "other" main character (I think you know who I mean). All others are very generic and interchangeable. You'll realize how basic everything is when you just rush a new game + for the achievements. I did this in 5 hours and I have no regrets missing out on any of the random things the game has to offer.


[b]Honourable mention:[/b]

And besides how simple and straight forward the game already is, they really have implemented a hand holding system from start to the very end of the game. Why? Just why? Do they really think gamers are just stupid and need constant advice not to get lost? I mean, it's ok in the beginning, but later it gets extremely annoying. 
You have to follow tracks but you will never lose them as they are highlighted like a Christmas tree in the evening. There is always a waypoint marker that points directly to the next quest step. There are almost 200 campfires (fast travel points and checkpoints) on the map, so you don't have to walk more than 50 meters. 200 of them! And Aloy is constantly commenting on things as you fight or walk around to remind you of the right path and tactics for specific enemies. 
[b]So, come on! Have a little faith in your customers. There are not deranged and certainly don't need constant guidance to beat your game. Do that!, Go there! I mean seriously![/b]

And before I forget. The AI ​​is really, really bad. Especially for the machines, but also for humans.


[b]Conclusion:[/b]

Those critics aside, the game is a wonderful pastime. But just don't expect any depth or great worldbuilding. It's wonderful for a first playthrough and maybe a second time for the story in a few years. But mostly I'm just disappointed with the lost potential and how bloated the game is. If you remove all that random stuff, you'll see that there just isn't much left.
But that's a problem of our time and people seemed content with this kind of games. Don't think much, don't ask much, just a time filler. Like a typical Hollywood action movie. You watch it and forget everything about it as soon as you leave the cinema. It's just not my thing. But stunning graphics and audio don't belie a thin concept and weak writting.

[b]Personal Score:[/b] 8/10

Ps.: Here's just a reminder. I was just talking about the bad stuff here. Because everything else has already been discussed many times. Graphics, audio, combat, weapons and the various elementals, mods, DLC are mostly top notch.

[quote][b]OVERVIEW[/b] ↴[/quote]
Horizon Zero Dawn is a third person/single player action game set in post-apocalyptic land ruled by mechanical creatures, in which the remains of humanity are split into warring tribes and kingdoms that dwell among the ruins of ancient times. And so here we are, in a regressed to a primitive state Earth, where we take on a role of a young huntress, an outcast of the Nora tribe, Aloy, who's forced by a series of events to go on a journey to not only uncover her past but also the origins of the world she currently lives in therefore the fall of the previous civilization.

[quote][b]GRAPHICS AND AUDIO[/b] ↴[/quote]
People can say a lot of different things about this game but we can all agree that as funny as it sounds, an apocalypse was never more beautiful and so visually stunning as it is in HZD which results in it being an absolute design masterpiece. I know, who would have thought.. Okay, I'm not kidding. The graphics alone can blow your mind. Sure, there are some tiny buggy things you can notice if you try hard enough (and you're a screenshot hoe) but it still doesn't diminish the fact that this apocalyptic world is simply breathtaking. From the lush and seemingly alive forests of Sacred Lands amongst the rippling of shining creeks and endlessly flowing rivers where sunlight strikes and glints on the gliding surface to the incredibly detailed snowy mountains from the great plateau to the captivating contrast between the days and nights which brings in a truly otherworldly lighting effects to this extraordinary environment.. Add now to this immersive graphics, an also impressive sound design which let's you with it's combination of flowing/soothing instrumental beats and mechanic sounds, draw you into a prehistoric yet futuristic life on Zero Dawn's Earth.
 
[quote][b]GAMEPLAY[/b] ↴[/quote]
The most pleasant surprise to me was how fluid and fun the gameplay actually is and beacuse of this, it simply went beyond my expectations. You've got an open world were exploration is always good and any kind of combat, whatever it be with machines, animals or humans is extremely rewarding but progressivly gets tougher the longer you get into the storyline which in itself is a pretty cool aspect. The mechanics of the combat are basically giving us a healthy challange in which we cannot always relay on one weapon through the whole game and makes us realize that it's sometimes best to switch your fighting style between stealh and full head-on attacks or just simply figure out each machine's attack pattern, capabilities and weaknesses to get a successful outcome without failing in the process or worse dying. Plus the fact that we can only save our progress in a campfire makes it all more exciting even if a bit cumbersome at times. The only thing that could deserve a criticism in this interesting game style would probably be the melee combat that feels like it has been added last minute as an afterthought from the devs to balance the heavy push on the player to use a long range combat instead.

[quote][b]STORY[/b] ↴[/quote]
We're set to immerse ourselves in a bit of self discovery mission for the main protagonist in this bizzare new world, all while trying to also uncover the truths about this strange corruption that's plaguing machines and wreaking havoc among Earth's remaining population. It's an exciting journey from the very start that leaves us with lots of interesting questions to the end where most of them are finally answered; it's filled with enough twists and turns to make it fun and immersive for any player dubbing themselves an RPG ethusiast. And to add a cherry on the top, the game offers us a large amount of side-missions, collectibles and challenges around the world to complete that in turn makes us stronger, thanks to a very generous XP and item rewards which doesn't leaves us with the impression of grinding for futher progress. Truly, a pretty well written story with a good dose of mystery to make the player enjoy and especially want to slowly piece together what happened to the Ancient Ones and the impacts of theirs decisions on the current state of Aloy's world but foremost what it means for her future. Ps. The atmposphere in this game is to die for, lol.

[quote][b]PERFORMANCE, BUGS AND GLITCHES[/b] ↴[/quote]
Ughh, there was the common problem that comes with a console games ported to pc which is the optimization. It was a bit of a problem since it resulted in lots of visual glitches, pretty low fps and some crashes that I've gotten to experience a lot when I started playing the game. But I can honestly say that since the last patch 1.06 HZD is running as smoothly as possible on my medium/high settings so I don't think anyone should have problems with running the game as it is right now 'cause it performs exceptionally well... But if you still get some crashes, it might help if you run the game .exe as admin instead of booting it up straight from steam and maybe putting the graphics on medium/low to balance the fact that this game loves to eat up players CPU like it's candy, no matter if you reach the minimum or high specs... I won't say anything about the camera having a mind of its own 'cause I truly didn't had any problems with it, so ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.

[quote][b]CONCLUSION[/b] ↴[/quote]
Horizon Zero Dawn: To hate it or to love it? In my opinion... love it. It's an amazing open world action game and a real treat that will give you a lot of hours to explore the vast and enchanting world of Zero Dawn with it's dangerous machines, and maybe not groundbreaking but very interesting storyline to follow; an absolute must play for action game fans that want an exciting journey to keep them at the edge of theirs seats with some of the best visuals available in gaming period.
